title: The history of lightning and thunder
tagline: From a thunder god's weapon to satellites that watch every flash.
intro: People first said lightning was a god's weapon. In ancient Greece and China, some began to look for natural causes. In 1752 a French rod and Franklin's kite showed it was electricity. Then cameras, radio and satellites showed how a stroke grows, how thunder forms, and how storms reach space. Some details are still argued over, and this history says so where it matters.

eras.name: Gods, breath and fire
eras.summary: Poets name a storm god. Greek and Chinese thinkers say lightning has natural causes.

eras.name: Sparks from the sky
eras.summary: Rods and kites show that lightning is electricity. Early lightning scientists risk their lives.

eras.name: Inside the storm
eras.summary: Cameras split a stroke into steps. Scientists ask how a cloud charges and whether it can be calmed.

eras.name: Above the clouds
eras.summary: Cameras and satellites find red sprites, gamma-ray flashes and beams of antimatter.

eras.name: Counting every flash
eras.summary: Radio networks and satellites count flashes, find hotspots and set new records.

events.title: Indra, lord of thunder
events.text: In the Rigveda, Indra is the god of storms, thunder and lightning. He carries the vajra, a thunderbolt, and kills the serpent Vritra to free the rain.
events.why: People first explained lightning as a god's weapon.

events.title: Aristotle blames a dry exhalation
events.text: In his Meteorology, Aristotle says a dry exhalation is squeezed out of cooling clouds and crashes into other clouds. That crash is thunder. When it catches fire as it escapes, it is lightning. We see the flash first because sight is quicker than hearing.
events.why: It was an early natural explanation, and it already knew that light beats sound.

events.title: Wang Chong says Heaven is not angry
events.text: In his Lunheng, the Han thinker Wang Chong argues that thunder and lightning are not Heaven's anger. Heaven, he says, acts without intent and has no hands to strike anyone. He also mocks the belief that lightning marks wrongdoers.
events.why: He asked people to test lightning stories against experience, not fear.

events.title: Franklin imagines the lightning rod
events.text: Franklin began to think about protecting buildings from lightning around 1750 and described a pointed iron rod. One source dates the idea to 1749. He suggested a sharp rod might draw off electricity before a strike.
events.why: It turned a physics idea into a way to save buildings.

events.title: Sparks from a storm cloud in France
events.text: Following Dalibard's instructions, a retired dragoon drew sparks from a 13 m insulated iron rod during a storm. Delor repeated the result in Paris. Dalibard reported it to the Académie des Sciences on 13 May.
events.why: It was the first time anyone tested Franklin's idea, and it showed that thunderclouds are electrified.

events.title: Franklin's kite
events.text: Franklin flew a kite in a storm and drew sparks from a key on the wet string. His own account came out in the Pennsylvania Gazette on 19 October 1752 and gave instructions for repeating it. The June date comes from Joseph Priestley's later telling, so details are uncertain.
events.why: It made the idea that lightning is electricity widely known.

events.title: Franklin wins the Copley Medal
events.text: The Royal Society gave Franklin its Copley Medal in 1753 for his experiments on electricity. Its members had earlier declined to print his lightning-conductor letter in the Philosophical Transactions.
events.why: It shows how fast the new idea won respect.

events.title: Richmann is killed by lightning
events.text: Richmann was measuring how an insulated rod reacted to a nearby storm. A discharge, reported to be ball lightning, struck him and he died. The French physicist Nollet used the death to argue against lightning rods.
events.why: It was a stark warning that studying lightning is dangerous.

events.title: Lomonosov's theory of storm electricity
events.text: Lomonosov had worked with Richmann since late 1744. After Richmann died, he wrote a discourse on air phenomena caused by electrical force. He proposed that friction between rising warm air and sinking cool air charges tiny particles.
events.why: It linked lightning to moving air inside the storm.

events.title: The first grounded rod in Moravia
events.text: Diviš, a priest, set up an iron frame of points on a tall wooden mast and grounded it with four iron chains. It is widely seen as the first rod that truly protected against lightning. Whether it was an independent invention is debated. Villagers destroyed it in 1760.
events.why: Grounding is what actually keeps a strike from damaging a building.

events.title: Blunt or pointed?
events.text: During the conflict between Britain and its American colonies, British scientists favoured rods with a ball on the end. American scientists favoured points. A study in 2000 found moderately blunt rods are marginally better receptors.
events.why: It shows even a simple rod has a design question.

events.title: Thunder becomes a shock wave
events.text: By the mid-1800s the accepted view was that lightning left a vacuum and thunder was its collapse. Since the 20th century, scientists agree that the channel heats the air so fast it expands as a shock wave. NOAA says it is a shock wave only for the first 10 yards, then ordinary sound.
events.why: It explains why thunder rolls and why it is not the same as a bang.

events.title: Wilson asks how electrons run away
events.text: In a 1925 paper, Wilson worked out how electrons can gain very large energy in a strong electric field such as a thundercloud's. Arthur Eddington later gave this the name runaway electrons.
events.why: It predicted high-energy radiation from storms decades before it was seen.

events.title: First estimate of global lightning
events.text: The first estimate of the global flash rate was 100 flashes per second. It was made in 1925 from the number of flashes per storm and storm counts at weather stations. Space-based counts later gave a mean of about 46 a second.
events.why: It started the long effort to count every flash on Earth.

events.title: Wilson's Nobel Prize
events.text: Wilson shared the 1927 Nobel Prize in Physics for the cloud chamber, which makes the paths of charged particles visible. His main interest was weather, and his work on thunderstorm electricity ran through his career. His last paper was about thunderclouds.
events.why: The inventor of a famous lab tool was a storm scientist at heart.

events.title: Schonland films the stepped leader
events.text: Schonland's team used Boys cameras with moving film. They split a stroke into stepped leader, return stroke and dart leader, and coined those terms. Step lengths of 10 to 200 m and an average speed of 3.8 × 10^5 m/s were reported.
events.why: It showed that lightning starts as a series of invisible-to-the-eye steps.

events.title: Vonnegut's convection theory
events.text: In 1954 Vonnegut proposed that strong up and down air currents are mainly what electrify a cloud. In 1946 he had also found that silver iodide can seed clouds. NOAA now says charge separation starts when soft hail called graupel collides with smaller ice crystals.
events.why: It put the storm's own winds at the centre of charging.

events.title: Project Skyfire tries to calm lightning
events.text: In 1956 Project Skyfire flew an airborne silver iodide generator on a Cessna 180 for about 60 hours. It also used ground generators near Flagstaff and Missoula. The aim was to cut lightning that starts forest fires.
events.why: It was an early test of whether people could change a storm's charging.

events.title: Sprites are caught on camera
events.who: Robert Franz, Robert Nemzek and John Winckler
events.text: University of Minnesota researchers were testing a low-light camera for a rocket experiment. It caught two flashes above a distant storm. Their 1990 Science paper reported a large upward discharge. Sources agree on 6 July, though one lists 4 July.
events.why: It proved that storms can flash up into space.

events.title: Winter lightning on Japan's coast
events.text: A Hokuriku Electric Power engineer described winter lightning along the Sea of Japan. It comes from warm sea air meeting cold Siberian winds, has long discharges and mostly strikes within about 35 km of the coast.
events.why: Power companies in Japan had to design for a different kind of lightning.

events.title: Gamma rays from thunderstorms
events.text: NASA's BATSE instrument first detected terrestrial gamma-ray flashes in 1994. It was built to study gamma-ray bursts from space. The flashes last about 0.2 to 3.5 milliseconds.
events.why: It was the first sign that lightning makes radiation.

events.title: A lightning camera in orbit
events.text: NASA launched the Optical Transient Detector in 1995. It was a prototype of the Lightning Imaging Sensor and flew as a hosted payload on a small satellite.
events.why: It began a satellite record that now spans decades.

events.title: The Lightning Imaging Sensor
events.text: The Lightning Imaging Sensor launched on the TRMM satellite in November 1997. It orbited at 350 km and watched a storm for about 90 seconds. The mission ended data collection on 8 April 2015.
events.why: It gave 17 years of total lightning data.

events.title: A world network of radio listeners
events.text: WWLLN uses more than 70 very low frequency radio sensors around the world. They hear radio pulses from strokes and locate each one from arrival times at five or more sensors. Its archive begins on 15 August 2004.
events.why: It lets scientists place strokes far out at sea.

events.title: Studying storm radiation on a mountain
events.text: In 2008 the cosmic ray division of the Yerevan Physics Institute began studying high-energy atmospheric physics on Mount Aragats. The station has recorded more than 500 bursts of particles since then.
events.why: It brought ground-based watching of storm radiation.

events.title: Thunderstorms fire antimatter
events.text: NASA's Fermi satellite saw gamma rays at 511,000 electron volts, a sign of electrons meeting positrons. On 14 December 2009 a beam from a storm in Zambia reached Fermi over Egypt. Fermi had found 130 flashes by the end of 2010.
events.why: It was the first direct evidence that storms make antimatter beams.

events.title: China reviews its lightning research
events.text: A review in Advances in Atmospheric Sciences describes ground-based field work on rocket-triggered lightning and thunderstorm electricity on the Tibetan Plateau. It says active research in China has run since the 1980s.
events.why: It collects work from a country with very different terrain.

events.title: The world's lightning capital
events.text: Sixteen years of satellite data showed that the top hotspot is over Lake Maracaibo, with 233 flashes per square kilometre a year. The Congo basin was second with 205.
events.why: It overturned the idea that Africa is always first.

events.title: A lightning mapper in geostationary orbit
events.text: GOES-16 carries the Geostationary Lightning Mapper. It sees all kinds of lightning day and night with about 10 km resolution and 20 second timing. It began operating in March 2017.
events.why: It lets forecasters watch lightning continuously.

events.title: Megaflash records
events.text: A flash on 31 October 2018 stretched 709 km across Brazil. One on 4 March 2019 lasted 16.73 seconds over Argentina. These more than doubled the previous records of 321 km (Oklahoma, 2007) and about 8 s (France, 2012). Satellites verified them.
events.why: Lightning can be far bigger than ground networks saw.

events.title: Records stretched again
events.text: The WMO listed a new distance record of 768 km across the southern United States on 29 April 2020. A flash on 18 June 2020 lasted 17.102 seconds over Uruguay and northern Argentina. Both were measured by GOES satellites.
events.why: The records keep rising as sensors improve.
